rows.claim: six browser agents score ~100% of items on fresh seeds with 0 model calls at 20-28 UI actions/s
rows.number: RECOVERED at much larger n from the live-wall recordings (eval/results/browser_agents_recovered.json): 102,899 episodes, 290,909/296,674 items = 98.06%, 0 model calls. Per task: shop 100.00%, desktop 100.00%, access 99.99%, chart 99.98%, recon 99.71%, inbox 94.39%
rows.source: eval/results/browser_agents.json holds only recon (125/125); the six-task bench file was overwritten. Recovered from $SP/live_run{6,7}.jsonl into eval/results/browser_agents_recovered.json
rows.environment_author: us (we wrote the five web apps AND the agents that solve them)
rows.grader: our code: window.__score() inside our own page, or our own checker
rows.agent_can_influence_grader: not directly (the score function is not exposed to perception), but same-author bias is total
rows.post_hoc_changes: YES, and the clearest case in the project: after the chart agent failed on pixel-identical bars, the chart GENERATOR was changed to redraw until the tallest bar is visibly tallest. NOW RESTORED: ties are possible again by default (99.5% on 400 fresh seeds, 2 abstentions, 0 wrong answers; 0/10 with 5 abstentions on the 5 known tie seeds), and the changed generator survives only as the opt-in ?ties=avoid. The access/chart retry relaxations were reviewed and are genuine correctness fixes: the cap on possibly-effectful attempts is still 3, and only attempts the app said had no effect are exempt.
rows.heldout_discipline: fresh seeds were used as a held-out set (seeds 2000-2150 after tuning on 1-40), which is real discipline; the recovered live runs cover ~103k episodes across unseen seeds; but the apps' difficulty distribution is ours
rows.control: none: no scrambled-agent or random-policy control was ever run on these apps
rows.note: The bench file was overwritten by a sibling's single-task re-run, so the quoted per-task tallies are gone; the same claim is recoverable from the live recordings at 750x the sample size (102,899 episodes) and holds at 98.06% overall with 0 model calls. What does NOT change: we wrote the apps, the graders inside them and the agents, and the chart generator was made easier after a failure — now restored to ties-possible by default and re-measured at 99.5% on 400 fresh seeds, with the changed version kept only as `?ties=avoid`. Large n against your own exam is still your own exam. Note the live figures are continuous-run episodes, not the bench harness, so seeds differ.

rows.claim: the desktop agent completes a multi-step shell chore and verifies it

rows.control: none
rows.note: State-based grading is a genuine step up from self-report. The task is still one we wrote for an agent we wrote.

rows.claim: the same desktop chore runs ~450x faster per episode on computerworld than on the browser-based simulator

rows.claim: fusing DOM and vision lifts word coverage; vision repairs a thinned accessibility tree

rows.claim: the grammar's coverage, measured by a set it did not author
rows.number: 193/193 cases pass: every claim shape the civilization's minds actually speak, crossed with four diverged dialects, asserting say->hear recovers predicate and object AND that the surface is well-formed English
rows.environment_author: us, but a DIFFERENT author than the grammar: the cases are generated from what research/civ_sim/minds.py actually puts into agents' mouths, not invented to exercise the parser
rows.grader: structural assertions (round-trip recovery; no doubled copula, no bare 'am' with a third-person subject, no partitive without 'of', no raw booleans, one full stop)
rows.agent_can_influence_grader: no; the demands come from the consumer, not the implementer
rows.post_hoc_changes: the grammar was fixed in response to this set, which is the normal direction; the set itself was generated from the sim's claim shapes, not tuned
rows.heldout_discipline: independent provenance rather than a held-out split: the consumer's needs were fixed before the grammar met them
rows.control: the fork's own 152-case act benchmark is the contrast, and it passed while this set failed
rows.note: This is the honest coverage measurement for src/tensacode/language, and it should be quoted instead of the act benchmark. It found five copula failures, a lost quantifier, a mis-stemmed verb, an inexpressible tense and a partitive gap: all in the commonest constructions, none on anyone's list.

rows.claim: a running world exposes defects no authored set catches (the credit side of the same pattern)
rows.number: fixing the grammar removed a spurious misunderstanding mechanism in the simulation: ungrammatical output counted as unfamiliar vocabulary, giving four common sentence types a ~45% chance of being misunderstood
rows.environment_author: us (two independent components, one consuming the other)
rows.grader: the simulation's own measured misunderstanding rate before and after
rows.post_hoc_changes: the defect was found by the consumer, not by the implementer's tests
rows.heldout_discipline: n/a
rows.control: before/after comparison of the misunderstanding rate
rows.note: Worth crediting because it is the mechanism working: one component we wrote held another to account, and it found something real. Two self-authored components checking each other is weaker than an outside grader but much stronger than one component grading itself.

rows.claim: the OCR fine-tune's removal of confident false successes (2 -> 0) held up
rows.number: it did not survive a change of environment: on computerworld all three recognizers make the same three errors, and the failures are lost hyphens, not the digit confusions the corpus targeted
rows.environment_author: us (task) in two different simulators
rows.grader: simulator state
rows.post_hoc_changes: the corpus was built to target the digit-confusion class observed in the OLD environment
rows.heldout_discipline: held-out fonts and apps for the crop metrics; the same 10 seeds for the end-to-end number
rows.control: three recognizers compared in the new environment, and they agree
rows.note: Same pattern as the language sets: a fix validated against the failure mode we had already seen, in the environment where we saw it. Moving environments produced a different failure class the corpus never covered. 2 -> 0 on ten episodes was two events; it should never have been quoted as a solved problem.

rows.claim: the grammar's authored test sets measured its coverage
rows.number: none of the fork's own authored sets contained a copular sentence with a third-person subject; every set it wrote passed, while a live world broke on five of its commonest sentence shapes
rows.environment_author: us
rows.grader: our expected readings
rows.agent_can_influence_grader: the same agent wrote the grammar and the cases that graded it
rows.post_hoc_changes: the bugs were found only when a running world used the grammar, not by any authored test
rows.heldout_discipline: none: the blind spot was systematic, so no amount of the same author's cases would have found it
rows.control: the civilization's 17 spoken shapes acted as an independent set and found five real bugs
rows.note: The sharpest demonstration in the project that self-authored test sets measure the author's imagination. A consumer we did not write found five bugs in the commonest constructions on first contact.

rows.claim: tensacode's cognition on public open-domain benchmarks, against the same model alone and a cascade
rows.number: rules: SQuAD2 9.1% @18.3% cov, HotpotQA 5.8% @91.3%, GSM8K 0.0% @5.3%, ARC-Easy 0% (refuses all). Model alone: 55.1% / 51.3% / 81.3% / 80.3%. Cascade WORSE than the model on 3 of 4. SQuAD2 rule arm 42.0% overall is below the 48.0% 'always abstain' floor
rows.environment_author: public datasets (SQuAD 2.0, HotpotQA distractor, GSM8K, ARC-Easy)
rows.grader: public labels; no model judged anything
rows.post_hoc_changes: none: the abstention threshold was chosen on a calibration slice disjoint from the test slice, and a test-slice threshold sweep is reported as a curve rather than tuned
rows.heldout_discipline: 300 test items per benchmark drawn from a fixed shuffle, 150 disjoint calibration items, Wilson CIs
rows.control: majority/frequency floor and a random control on every benchmark, a forced-guess variant on ARC-Easy, plus a plain-model arm and an equal-coverage comparison
rows.note: The least flattering measurement in the project and the most independent. It disconfirms the cascade story off home turf: a cheap tier whose abstention is capability-blind makes the system worse than the model alone.
